Wah gwan, noah? Di archives speak of a time when babylon’s authorities, determined to fit a crime, introduced new laws to track and monitor Marcus Garvey’s movements in the hope of reversing the African Diaspora’s improvements. Yet through newspapers, property businesses, and an emerging shipping line, the principle of steadfast organization and self-reliance endured, proving that persecution signals the threat our unity poses to those in power. Wi must rise with the same unyielding determination that defined the movement, for the records show how J Edgar Hoover employed the FBI’s first African American informant to infiltrate and spy, leading to a 1923 sentence of five years for suspected mail fraud.

That historical application reveals Garvey’s will to deliver more than just hope remained unquestionable. After serving two years, he immediately returned to Jamaica to continue educating the people dem, an insistence that could not be silenced by propaganda claiming his methods were flawed. From there he created the People’s Political Party in 1928—the first political party to defend the interests of Jamaica’s African Caribbean community—before traveling to England, where he addressed crowds at Speaker’s Corner without ever forgetting who he represented. The archives make clear that external pressures sharpened rather than halted the resolve to build institutions that educated and mobilized millions.

Tek note, noah, that such resilience offers practical wisdom for today: di people dem cannot wait for kinder times but must answer surveillance and adversity with renewed political and educational structures. The core principle of self-reliance teaches that any claim of impossibility echoes the doubts Garvey’s enemies hoped to sow, yet those doubts were overcome by persistent labor in the face of imprisonment and monitoring. This layered truth—principle forged in history, applied through organization—empowers the African Diaspora to recognize that true advancement comes through transparent self-governance amid babylon’s schemes.

To put this into action, first establish or strengthen a local discussion circle modeled on the People’s Political Party’s defense of community interests, because the records show this step counters infiltration by fostering transparent self-governance. Second, commit to weekly circulation of community writings in the spirit of the newspapers Garvey built, for the archives demonstrate how printed propaganda educated and mobilized despite official monitoring. Third, defend community interests through a structured political body akin to the 1928 party, since the evidence records that Garvey returned from imprisonment to found exactly such an instrument of lasting power.
